content: Performance status is a clinical metric used in oncology and other medical fields to assess the overall well-being and functional capacity of cancer patients. This evaluation helps determine whether a patient is fit to undergo chemotherapy, whether adjustments to the treatment dose are necessary, and the level of palliative care required. Scoring Systems Several scoring systems are employed to evaluate performance status. The most widely used are the Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS) and the ECOG/WHO/Zubrod scale. For pediatric patients, the Lansky Performance Scale is commonly utilized. Other related scoring systems include the Global Assessment of Functioning (GAF) score, which is part of the fifth axis in the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM). Karnofsky Performance Scale (KPS) The Karnofsky Performance Scale ranges from 100% to 0%, with 100% representing perfect health and 0% indicating death. Although the scale is typically divided into 10-point intervals, clinicians may use decimal values to more precisely describe a patient’s condition. The scale was developed by Dr. David A. Karnofsky and Dr. Joseph H. Burchenal in 1949. The specific levels are as follows: 100%: The patient is in normal health, has no complaints, and shows no signs of disease. 90%: The patient is capable of normal activity but may have minor symptoms or signs of disease. 80%: The patient can perform normal activities but experiences some difficulty and has noticeable symptoms or signs. 70%: The patient is able to care for themselves but is not capable of engaging in normal activities or work. 60%: The patient requires some assistance but can manage most personal needs independently. 50%: The patient frequently requires help and medical care. 40%: The patient is disabled and needs special care and assistance. 30%: The patient is severely disabled, requires hospital admission, but is not at immediate risk of death. 20%: 10%: The patient is moribund, with rapidly progressing fatal disease processes. 0%: The patient is deceased. ECOG/WHO/Zubrod Performance Scale The ECOG Performance Scale, also known as the WHO or Zubrod scale, was introduced by Oken et al. in 1982. It ranges from 0 to 5, with 0 indicating perfect health and 5 representing death. The scale is defined as follows: 0: The patient is asymptomatic and fully active. 1: The patient has symptoms but remains fully ambulatory. 2: The patient has symptoms and spends less than 50% of the day in bed. 3: The patient has symptoms and spends more than 50% of the day in bed but is not completely bedbound. 4: The patient is completely bedbound. 5: The patient is deceased. Lansky Performance Scale The Lansky Performance Scale is specifically designed for children, who may have difficulty articulating their quality of life. This observational scoring system was proposed and validated by Lansky et al. in 1987. The scale ranges from 100 to 0, with the following descriptions: 100: The child is fully active and exhibits normal behavior. 90: The child has minor restrictions in performing strenuous physical activities. 80: The child remains active but tires more quickly than usual. 70: The child has greater restrictions in play and spends less time engaging in play activities. 60: The child is up and moving but engages minimally in active play, preferring quieter activities. 50: The child spends much of the day lying down but gets dressed and participates in quiet play and activities. 40: The child is mostly confined to bed but can still engage in quiet activities. 30: The child is bedbound and requires assistance even for quiet play. 20: The child sleeps most of the time, with play limited to very passive activities. 10: The child does not play or get out of bed. 0: The child is unresponsive.
